events.title: Microsoft and the US government propose a settlement
events.description: The agreement would restrict some business practices. Court review and other legal steps remain.

events.title: Euro cash enters everyday use
events.description: Twelve countries introduce euro notes and coins.

events.title: Columbia is lost
events.description: The space shuttle breaks apart during its return to Earth, killing its seven crew members.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina strikes
events.description: The hurricane devastates Gulf Coast communities and creates an enormous need for rescue and recovery.

what_happened_next.text:
Microsoft led this set, with the international basket close behind. PepsiCo gained, but Coca-Cola lost about one-quarter of its value. The US basket finished slightly behind cash. Two companies selling similar products did not give investors the same result, and a crowded news month did not supply a clear answer.

In November 2001, Microsoft and the US government proposed a settlement of their competition case. The legal story had moved forward, though review was still required.

Euro notes and coins began circulating in 2002. The Columbia shuttle was lost in 2003, and Hurricane Katrina devastated Gulf Coast communities in 2005. Scientific work, everyday business and terrible disasters all formed part of these years. No single headline captured everything investors would face.

Coca-Cola and PepsiCo are an important contrast. Both sold familiar drinks, yet their shares did not deliver the same result. Buying a product often is different from knowing what its company’s stock will be worth later. The international basket offered another mix of businesses and currencies. Compare those choices with your own reasons at the start: which reasons were sensible, and which depended on a future you could not actually see?

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: The presidential election was finally settled. Drink makers chased new markets, and scientists studied signs of ancient water on Mars.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Similar brands could take different paths. The international share basket added businesses outside the US, with different opportunities, risks and currencies.
reflection.what_faded_away: A new drink deal or a year-end economic prediction could not settle the five-year ranking. The story continued long after the headlines changed.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew the exact company outcomes or the shocks ahead. A familiar household product was not a guarantee against losing money.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: PepsiCo completed its Quaker Oats purchase in August 2001, adding Gatorade to its drinks business. By 2005, Gatorade and Aquafina were growing strongly, helped by new flavours and warm weather. North American beverage sales rose 10% that year, while Frito-Lay’s sales also grew. Selling snacks, sports drinks and bottled water gave PepsiCo several sources of growth behind its stock gain.

Coca-Cola’s size did not guarantee fast growth. In 2004, North American drink volume was flat, and its new C2 drink sold less well than expected. Coca-Cola Zero arrived in 2005, helping improve results, and worldwide drink volume grew 4% that year. The business was still growing, but that progress did not translate into a gain from this window’s starting share price.

Microsoft expanded beyond Windows and Office while its main software businesses kept producing cash. By June 2005, annual sales reached $39.79 billion, helped by server software and Xbox growth. The company also returned $44 billion to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks during that financial year. Growing earnings and cash payments helped this later starting point finish with a gain.
